approachQuestion.prompt:
One unmatched token

A read-only nondecreasing random-access integer array has odd length. Exactly one distinct value appears once; every other distinct value appears exactly twice. Return the value appearing once. 1<=n<=200001. Examples: [2,2,4,7,7] -> 4; [5] -> 5; [1,1,3,3,8] -> 8. Prefer worst-case probes, then memory.
constraints: Use only the stated input ordering and access guarantees.

options.text: Keep lo=0,hi=n-1. While lo<hi, choose midpoint and round it down to an even index. If a[mid]==a[mid+1], set lo=mid+2; otherwise set hi=mid. Return a[lo].
options.feedback: Pairs start at even indices before the singleton and odd indices after it, turning parity into a search predicate.

options.text: Run the same parity-based search recursively on index bounds.
options.feedback: This returns the unique singleton, but recursion retains avoidable stack frames.

options.text: Return the middle element without inspecting pair alignment.
options.feedback: For [1,1,2,2,3,4,4], the middle element is 2, but the singleton is 3.

details: Keep lo=0,hi=n-1. While lo<hi, choose midpoint and round it down to an even index. If a[mid]==a[mid+1], set lo=mid+2; otherwise set hi=mid. Return a[lo]. Pairs start at even indices before the singleton and odd indices after it, turning parity into a search predicate.

Before the singleton, equal pairs start at even positions; afterward their alignment shifts by one. Rounding midpoint down to even makes the adjacent comparison expose that transition. Discard a complete matching pair, not one member.

“Keep lo=0,hi=n-1. While lo<hi, choose midpoint and round it down to an even index. If a[mid]==a[mid+1], set lo=mid+2; otherwise set hi=mid. Return a[lo].”: Pairs start at even indices before the singleton and odd indices after it, turning parity into a search predicate.

“Return the middle element without inspecting pair alignment.”: For [1,1,2,2,3,4,4], the middle element is 2, but the singleton is 3.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For target-method, choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Analyze the iterative even-midpoint algorithm, not an XOR scan. Random access and integer operations are constant time, with no copies or recursion. Input storage and returned result storage are excluded; all temporary buffers and call stacks are included.
constraints: Use worst-case bounds. Count all working memory including any stack; exclude supplied inputs and the scalar result.

feedback.reason: Parity-aligned comparisons halve the candidate range around the singleton.
details: Even-midpoint comparisons discard a completed pair and a contiguous half of candidates. O(log(n+1)) iterations locate the singleton using only low, high, and midpoint. Unlike an XOR solution, this fixed method does not scan every element.
“O(log(n + 1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Pairs start at even indices before the singleton and odd indices after it, turning parity into a search predicate.
“O(n*n + 1) time, O(n + 1) auxiliary space”: Even-aligned probes eliminate matching pairs and halve the range; they neither enumerate pairs nor store an n-entry table.
“O(1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: A singleton can lie at any valid transition location, requiring multiple parity-guided midpoint probes.
